author: Clicked
text:
Some good stuff there, trying to dig out the dyno data from those old threads and compare it with shim stack tuning theories to see if any of those theories make any sense. There are four theories on why tall stacks are stiffer. Each theory is a little different.

  

 From the Belleville spring equation the stiffness of shims increase with deflection due to the build up of internal strain within the shim material. At the same edge lift thin shims create larger internal strains making thin shims stiffer.  

 From the stacked bowl theory, the stack structure becomes stiffer due to the forced sharper bend radius at the top of the stack. The stiffness of the individual shims remains the same.

 The fulcrum theory shows the face shims become stiffer due to the larger projected clamp diameter through a tall stack.

  

 In that respect the fulcrum theory is opposite of the stacked bowl theory. The stacked bowl theory asserts the sharper bend radius at the top of the stack makes the top of the stack stiffer. The fulcrum theory asserts the larger projected clamp diameter makes the face shim stiffer. Either way, tall stacks are stiffer but for opposite reasons.

 Both of those theories are based on things going on in the stack structure that make the structure stiffer then the sum of the individual shims assumed by shim factors. The Belleville spring theory asserts thin shims are just flat stiffer regardless of the stack structure.

  

 Which ever theory you chose, the MXScandinavia dyno data shows there are things going on in the shim stack that cause the stiffness of the structure to be different than the sum of the individual shim stiffness. The projected clamp fulcrum and stacked bowl effect caused shim factors to under estimated the stiffness of thin face shims, over estimate thick shims and get the change in stiffness direction wrong for the stacks dyno tested here.  

Shim stack stiffness depends on two things:
The stiffness of the shims

The stiffnesss of the stack structure.

 When the stack structure interacts with the stiffness of the individual shims it makes it hard to figure out the actual stiffness of a shim stack using shim factors. The MXScandinavia dyno data has shown examples of that.

author: Clicked
text:
Webology: A tall stack of thin shims is stiffer than a short stack of thick shims

  

 True. The fulcrum theory, internal shim strain, shim friction, stacked bowl theory and the MXScandinavia dyno data all show a tall stack of thin shims is stiffer than a short stack of thick shims. Differences in stack surface area, non-linear shim stiffness and the way forces are transferred through the shim stack structure alter the shim bend profile and the effective stiffness of shims making tall stacks stiffer. Those effects are not included in shim factor theory.

author: Clicked
text:
Webology: A short stack of thick shims is more progressive than a tall stack of thin shims

  

 False. The stacked bowl theory and the fulcrum theory both claim a tall stack of thin shims is stiffer. The stacked bowl theory also asserts shims at the top of the stack are forced to bend around a sharper bend radius as lift increases. That makes tall stacks become progressively stiffer as lift increases. 

  

 That theory is backed up by the MXScandinavia dyno data and finger press data. Both show a tall stack of thin shims is stiffer than a theoretically equivalent short stack of thick shims scaled by shim factors. The finger press data also shows shim stacks become progressively stiffer as lift increases backing up the progressive stiffness increase expected by the stacked bowl theory.

 [[IMG:7-finger-press.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/7-finger-press.png.cddd06f58c12317a07ef9ef4aa85ded8.png]]

author: Clicked
text:
Tall Stacks Are Stiffer

 The first two dyno test series from MXScandinavia checked out the use of shim factors for tuning a stack. The first test modified the face shims and the second test modified the stack taper. Results of those tests demonstrated an important point: Simple changes to a shim stack do not produce a simple result. The actual stiffness of a shim stack structure is different than a simple sum of the individual shim stiffness.

 Now that we know a little more about the influence of a shim stack structure on the overall stiffness of a shim stack based on the fulcrum and stacked bowl theory we need to go back and look at the test data from the first MXScandinavia dyno test again.

 [[IMG:7-finger-press.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/7-finger-press.png.cddd06f58c12317a07ef9ef4aa85ded8.png]]

 Based on shim factors those two stacks were setup to be theoretically equivalent. The dyno test data, finger press and FEA analysis all showed the SF14 stack was stiffer with a difference in the 20% range at high lift. Review of that test data was focus on verifying the MXScandinavia dyno data against the Ohlins factory data and verifying both of those data sources against the finger press measurements. Data from each of those tests provided an independent validation of the other giving some confidence in the measurements and the result. All of that test data and the FEA results showed the SF14 stack was stiffer then expected by shim factor theory. The “why” of that difference and the “why” of shim factors mucking up the stack stiffness estimate was left hanging.

 Now that we know a little more about shim stack theory we can go back and look at those two stacks and understand the SF14 stack was stiffer because it was taller. That difference is a result of the fulcrum theory, stacked bowl theory, non-linear shim stiffness, shim friction or some combination of all four effects. The bottom line is tall stacks are stiffer. The dyno data from that first test series is a second example demonstrating that point and a second example demonstrating the structural stiffness of a shim stack is different than a simple sum of the individual shim stiffness. That difference was 20% at high lift, so it is an important effect.

 The other important thing to point out here is data from the first MXScandinavia test demonstrated a tall stack of face shims is stiffer than a short stack. Dyno data from the second test series demonstrated a tall tapered section of the stack is stiffer than a short one. It makes no difference what section of the stack is taller. Tall stacks are just flat stiffer.

author: Clicked
text:
High Speed Stack

 Enough theory, lets look at some dyno data for practical suspension tuning problems

 

“Loosen up high speed damping by pulling the even number shims from the high speed stack, unless you be fast – then pull the odd.”

  

 That statement is spread all over suspension forums. Others say shim stacks don't work that way, the high speed stack effects damping force everywhere, not just at high speed.

 So whats the deal? Do high speed stack changes make a difference or not?

  

 MXScandinavia posted some dyno data on TT showing what modification to the high speed stack do in terms of changing the shape of the damping force curve. This first example keeps the same low speed stack and replaces five 0.25 mm shims in the high speed stack with softer 0.20 mm thick shims. That mod keeps the same number of shims in the stack so the shim surface area and friction should be the same for both stacks.

 [[IMG:1-mx3c.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/1-mx3c.png.0b11fd3a975be189a79826b663e5976e.png]]

 By the thickness cubed rule 0.20 mm shims have 51% of the stiffness of a 0.25 mm shim. The stack has ten shims in the stack taper and this mod replaces five of them with 51% softer shims. So half of the shims in the stack taper were replaced with shims that were half as stiff. So maybe that loosens up the high speed stack by 25% or so?

  

 Does softening the high speed stack loosen up high speed damping or not?

author: mog
text: Yes but it affects the low speed by a smaller margin

author: Clicked
text:
Tapered Shim Factors

  

 To get a guess on how the dyno test might turn out here is some tapered shim factor info. Both stacks have the same number of face shims so the low speed stiffness of the two stacks should be the same, at least some think that way. The high speed tapered section of the mx4c stack uses thicker 0.25 mm shims. Sum up the shim factors for the high speed stack and the mx4c configuration has a tapered shim factor of 126.

 The modified configuration, mx3c, replaces the 38 through 30 mm shims in the stack taper with thinner 0.20 mm shims. That drops the shim factor for the high speed tapered section to 88. Compare that to 126 for the baseline stack and the modified high speed stack should be 30% softer.

 [[IMG:2-mx3c.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/2-mx3c.png.283f45e3159cc4e28368fb426aafe7eb.png]]

 Sum up the entire stack and the tapered shim factor for the baseline stack is 219. That gets reduced to 180 with the replacement shims in the mx3c stack making the overall stack 18% softer.

 Tapered Stack Shim Factors

 Same low speed stack

 High speed stack 30% softer

 Overall stack 18% softer

 Nothing subtle there, those are some big changes to the stack. Does loosening up the high speed stack soften high speed damping and change the shape of the damping force curve or not?

author: Clicked
text:
Dyno Test Results:

 The goal here was loosen up high speed damping by replacing five 0.25 mm shims in the stack taper with softer 0.20 mm shims. By shim factors that should soften the high speed stack by 30%. The dyno shows damping force was only reduced by 9%. Shim factors missed the change in high speed damping by a factor of 3.

  

 Sum up shim factors for the entire stack and the overall stack stiffness should have been reduced by 18%. The dyno shows 9% softer compression damping. Shim factors missed the change in overall damping force by a factor of 2.

  

 What about the shape of the damping force curve? The dashed blue line on the plot below takes the mx3c dyno data points and multiplies by 1.088. That dashed line runs right through the mx4c data points and the FEA curve for that stack. The data shows no difference in the shape of the damping force curve between those two stacks. Modifying the high speed stack just made the damping force softer and it was softer everywhere, not just at high speed.

 [[IMG:3-mx3c-dyno.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/3-mx3c-dyno.png.a4d3bb71ecfc58359009c3c6b6fae63c.png]]

 The general webology thinking is replacing those five 0.25 mm shims in the stack taper with softer 0.20 mm shims should have really loosened up the high speed stack and high speed damping for better wheel compliance. The dyno shows the 30% shim factor change in the high speed stack only produced a 9% difference in damping force and the damping force got softer everywhere, not just at high speed. The dyno data shows the high speed stack works a whole lot different than the general webology thinking of high speed shim stack tuning.

author: Clicked
text:
High Speed Dyno Data

 The dyno data from that test goes out to shaft speeds of 120 in/sec. For a 3:1 shock linkage that shaft speed works out to a suspension wheel velocity of 360 in/sec (9.1 m/sec). From the bump velocity plot we looked at earlier (linky) a dyno shaft speed of 120 in/sec is equivalent to hitting an 8” bump at 30 mph, or a 4” bump at about 50 mph. That's definitely in the high speed range where modifications to the high speed stack should have shown up in the dyno data. The dyno did not show that. Instead, the dyno shows modifying the high speed stack just makes the damping force softer and it was softer everywhere over the entire speed range, not just at high speed.

 [[IMG:4-hs-mods.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/4-hs-mods.png.03642a52e1c8104ff578ecf3e4d9ff9f.png]]

 Both of those stacks had a crossover, so you'd think changes to the high speed stack would have been separate from changes to the low speed stack. They are not. Changing the high speed stack changes the damping force everywhere, not just at high speed.

 It is possible to setup a crossover to separate low speed and high speed damping. To separate the speed ranges you have to use a special crossover configuration Jeremy Wilkey (linky) on dirt rider defines as a non-interactive crossover. TT has a bunch of dyno data comparing different crossover configurations and the effect different crossover styles have on the shape of the damping force curve. We will look at that dyno data later and try to figure out what crossover configuration modifications you have to make to separate the speed ranges.

author: harrperf
text:
It makes you wonder why we bother with cross overs that don't in any way separate high and low speed ,and for the most part are acting like a single stage ?

  

  

 I do believe the ultra low speed is affected - and it may provide an "out" for friction...separating the upper and lower enough to remove the friction component some.

 If the "low" speed cross over is smaller than clamp shim I also feel it's more pronounced of a cross over.

  

 Lastly, We run preloaded stacks in some cases - however to precisely get a small amount of preload that does what we want is hard the way i do it.  Instead I feel it's more consistent to run a little more preload/taper for machining purposes but then use a cross over to prevent the entire stack from being preloaded.  Of course this requires the cross over thickness be sufficient to leave room for the upper stack to flex the preloaded amount before hitting the lower stack - and in many cases the cross over be smaller than the clamp shim.

  

  

 I've actually found a very good level of success with "soft" stacks with decent preload for faster riders in outdoors...getting the balance of high speed bump absorption but enough area under the damping curve to handle these guys speed is tough without boosting the early parts of the curve - but not the bleed circuits which will often translate to harshness.  I think forks for fast guys are different - Decent low speed bleed (soft) but limited peak mid valve deflection adn relatively stiff midvalve seems to work well.

author: Clicked
text:
Good discussion. From the dyno data it is not clear if the crossover gap in those two stacks does anything. Maybe, on an ultra high speed impulse blow, the gap allows the outside edge of the stack to blow off. But the dyno curve shows no evidence of that and no evidence of the stiffer stiffer high speed shims making the damping force stiffer at high speed.

  

 Tall Stacks Are Stiffer (Sometimes)

 The “tall stacks are stiffer” theory is worth thinking about here. The first MXScandinavia dyno test replaced a stack of 14x40.2 face shims with a shim factor equivalent stack of 4x40.3 face shims. That reduced the overall shim stack height by 29%. The shorter stack was supposed to have the same stiffness but tested to be 20% softer at high lift on the finger press. That gave some credibility to the fulcrum theory, stack bowl theory and the idea that “tall stacks are stiffer”.

  

 The second test replaced eleven 0.20 mm shims in the stack taper with softer pairs of 0.15 mm shims. Based on shim factors that stack was theoretically 5% softer but dyno tested to be 3% stiffer. The change in stack height for that test was 22% and gave a second example verifying the “tall stacks are stiffer” theory.

  

 The dyno test above replaced five 0.25 mm shims in the high speed stack tapered section with softer 0.20 mm shims. By shim factors that should have made the stack 18% softer. The thinner 0.20 mm shims also made the stack 5% shorter. The shorter stack should have been even more than 18% softer based on the “tall stacks are stiffer” theory.

  

 But the dyno did not show that. The dyno showed the difference in damping force was only 9%. Not the 18% estimated by shim factors, or an even greater difference based on the “tall stacks are stiffer” theory. Apparently, a 5% change in stack height is not enough to bring the “tall stacks are stiffer” theory into play compared to the 29% and 22% stack height change of the first two tests. There is something else going on in the stack structure of those two shim stacks that makes the stiffness difference less than expected by shim factors and in the opposite direction expected by the “tall stacks are stiffer” theory.

One week and no word from GD. He must have gotten lucky, or really unlucky, at the bar.

 Here is where we are at: Replaced five shims in the stack taper with thicker 0.25mm shims. Based on shim factors the replacement shims should increase the stiffness of the high speed stack by 40%.

 [[IMG:5-mx9c.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/5-mx9c.png.771d9b07302389702ad9b4cad88da6af.png]]

 FEA Analysis

 So what about FEA analysis? If you ran FEA on the two stacks what does that say about the difference in stiffness between the two stacks?

 FEA computes the shim stack deflection as a function of force applied to the stack. At a given force you can integrate around the perimeter of the valve port seat and get a measure of the fluid flow area between the shim stack and valve seat at the computed stack deflection. Do that over a range of stack forces and you get a curve showing how the fluid flow area changes with stack force.

 For the stacks here FEA shows the shim stack deflection profile is pretty linear for both stacks. The difference in stiffness is also nearly constant. That means there is not going to be any difference in the shape of the damping force curve between the two stacks. The mx10c stack is just stiffer and produces about 10% less flow area over the deflection range. That's a whole lot different than shim factors that expected a 40% increase in stack stiffness at high speed.

 [[IMG:6-mx9c-fea.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/6-mx9c-fea.png.d34e47de94fa3fee3997288dd886d6ac.png]]

 The FEA calculations show the mx9c stack is about 10% softer. That means when the shock is producing the same damping force, with the same pressure drop across the valve, the softer mx9c stack is going to deflect to a 10% larger flow area. With 10% more flow area the shock is going to have to operate at a 10% higher shaft speed to produce 10% more fluid flow to fill that increased area. With that thinking the mx9c stack should match the damping force of the mx10c stack when the mx9c stack is operated at a 10% higher shaft velocity.

 Tapered Stack Shim Factors

 40% stiffer at high speed

 16% stiffer overall

author: Clicked
text:
Webology:

The low speed stack controls low speed damping

The high speed stack controls high speed damping

 Those basic shim stack tuning webology ideas make a lot of sense when you look at the structure of a shim stack with a crossover. The face shims control low speed damping and the tapered section controls high speed damping. Simple. But, most shim stack don't work that way.

 [[IMG:8-crossover.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/8-crossover.png.0d95d6630948e9c16c2b79a9bc20fc5e.png]]

 Most crossovers use a shim diameter that is larger than the stack clamp. The larger crossover transfers some of the force from the low speed stack directly into the high speed stack before the crossover closes. That forces the high speed stack to start deflecting before the crossover closes.

  

 Crossovers are configured that way on purpose. Force transfer through the crossover into the high speed stack smooths the crossover closure transition, so there is no sharp kink in the damping force curve when the crossover closes. That smooths the crossover closure transition and creates a shim stack structure where everything interacts and there is no separate low speed or high speed stack. Dyno data from the last two test series demonstrate that point.  

			
				

	Edited July 20, 2015 by Clicked

author: Clicked
text:
Valving Logic has done those kind of tests, but that proprietary data has not been posted on TT as far as I know.

  

 From an analytical standpoint there are two components to stack torque: If any shim is not analytically flat it is going to take some clamp torque to flatten the bent, warped or pretzeled shims. Flip any of those bent shims over and the stack is going to go from preloaded to floated and change the damping force measured on a dyno.

  

 The other component is dirt or lint trapped in the stack. To test for that run the first test as a baseline. Disassemble, re-torque the stack and repeat the test. Any dirt or lint in the stack is partially ground up by the first test so the second test clamps the stack a little better. Of coarse, dirt or lint trapped in the stack has nothing to do with damping force repeatability. It just bad test technique.

  

 The bottom line is trying to A/B shim stack configurations on a dyno requires a good test technique run in a clean environment. The other way to insure the data integrity is combine dyno testing with analysis as this thread is doing. When the dyno data lines up with analysis you have some confidence the data is good. When they don't line up you need to spend a little bit of time trying to figure out the why of that.

  

 For the MXScandinavia tests the dyno data for changes to the face shims or the high speed stack line up with the changes expected from FEA analysis. Test and analysis are all consistent. Whats not working out is all of these webology rules of thumb – like the high speed stack controls high speed damping. That's not analysis - its just folk lore and it does not work. The dyno data from both MXScandinavia and Valving Logic show that.

The dyno shows mog02 was about 28% stiffer at 10 in/sec and held that stiffness across the entire speed range to end up 25% stiffer at high speed. Adding face shims to the mog02 stack increased the damping force everywhere, not just at low speed.

 [[IMG:13-mog-dyno.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/13-mog-dyno.png.d0f6a7f39adf87412c828b983636e1e8.png]]

 The mog03 stack used a smaller clamp. The thinking there was the smaller clamp should offset the added face shims and drop the low speed damping to be 4% to 7% softer then mog01. Then at high speed the smaller clamp should have made mog03 12% to 15% softer compared to mog01. Test results show mog03 was about 15% softer at low speed and stayed softer to end up 17% softer at high speed. The dyno shows the mog03 stack was softer everywhere, not just at high speed.

 [[IMG:14-dyno-table.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/14-dyno-table.png.1fe9164916301f452acc8b38d2ba329e.png]]

 Neither stack matches the changes expected from webology or the tapered shim factor equation. Increasing the low speed stack stiffness or decreasing the high speed stack makes little difference in the shape of the damping force curve. The stacks were either softer or stiffer and that difference remained relatively constant over the entire speed range. Here's Mog's conclusion:

"You have shown to a reasonable degree that if we add face shims we get a similar curve moved up, and if we remove damping via the clamp we move the curve down, the shape and angle is similar, so overall conclusion is it doesn't matter which end of the stack you work with, the effects are similar for the curve."

  

 Results of the TT MXScandinavia dyno thread was from six years ago. Today, six years latter, nothing much has changed in the webology of shim stack tuning. The high speed stack and low speed stack are still talked about and tuned as if they were separate things that can be independently tuned to separately control high speed and low speed damping. Shim stack don't work that way, the dyno data and FEA results both show that.

 

 There is an exception. On dirt rider, Jeremy Wilkey defines two separate styles of crossover shim stacks: interactive and non-interactive. It is possible to separate low speed and high speed damping but you have to use a special crossover configuration Wilkey defines as a non-interactive crossover. TT has a whole bunch of dyno data demonstrating effects of different crossover styles. We will look at that data latter as well as stack preload effects. With stack preload, low speed damping and the shape of the damping force curve can be modified far more than most tuners realize.

author: harrperf
text:
The biggest issue is people dont often see shims as a spring..

 But if thought about as a single rate coil spring... Then adjusting the damping curve is a matter of spring rate, preload, and bleed, then lastly piston port effects and inlet conditions, seal drag, mechanical drag... Viscous drag, which of course is damping of its own variety.

 I watched a nice promotional video from penske shocks... They work mostly to produce dampers with minimal seal drag, minimal hysterisis, and if course the damping curves and shapes they need via piston and stack design.

 The bigger picture questions for me have become honing in on damping settings that match a specific bike and chassis, linkage and leverage ratio.. And then of course a rider. 

 Identical forks made to fit different brands of bikes feel different on each bike. The chassis plays a critical role.

 Then the linkages role in my opinion can not be overlooked. What velocity region the shock shaft sees... Most notably at low wheel speeds plays a tremendous role in feel and performance to the rider

 An example is two extremes... If a linkage has very large leverage.. As an example lets say 10:1... The shaft velocity range is reduced by a factor of 10.

 This could be desireable if the damper had a large progression of damping force vs velocity.

 By limiting shaft velocity range we keep damping force in a range we want.

 But a negative could be at low shaft speeds... With a lack of fluid velocity we dont have good control and precision of tuning.

 I think finding the perfect blend of damper characteristics and leverage ratio could make all the difference

author: Clicked
text:
Damping Force Curve Shape

 There are three shapes to a damping force curve. The shape refers to whether damping force increase more or less than a linear curve.

 Linear: Damping force increases linearly with shaft speed (straight line)

 Progressive: Damping force increases more than a linear curve (curve hooks upward)

 Digressive: Damping force increases less than a linear curve (curves downward)

 [[IMG:18-curve-shape.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/18-curve-shape.png.b0dd02106a7c988be87e8350f7efc977.png]]

 The three curves above are simply the shaft velocity raised to some power (pow= 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3) and were setup so damping force matches at 20 in/sec. That makes the digressive curve produce more damping force at low speed and less damping force at high speed. The progressive curve does the opposite.

 Shocks are setup to produce a digressive damping force curve. The reason for that is the shock needs to produce heavy damping force at low speed for control of the chassis and light damping forces at high speed to allow the wheels to float over bumps.

  

 With that understanding of damping force curve shape the damping coefficient data for mog's stacks shows the shock was progressive from zero to 5 in/sec and then went digressive at higher shaft speeds.  

 [[IMG:19-mog-coeff.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/19-mog-coeff.png.f0fd9db5d3a65c33210b95eda5a947cf.png]]

 The reason for the shift in curve shape is the shim stack is closed at zero velocity and all of the flow is force through the clickers. The fixed orifice flow circuit of the clickers makes the low speed curve progressive. Above 5 in/sec the shim stack cracks open and the damping force curves went digressive.

 Hack around on the shim stack configurations and you could make those curves above 5 in/sec progressive or even more digressive.

  

 If you followed that you can understand the discussion of curve shape can get really confusing. Shocks are going to start out with a progressive curve when on the bleed circuits and then transition to some other shape as the bleed circuits fight it out with the shim stack/valve port configuration.

 That is where plotting out the data as a damping coefficient really helps out to understand the curve shape as well as what is going on in the shock. If the damping coefficient increases with shaft speed the curve is progressive. If it decreases the curve is digressive. Simple.

			
				

	Edited August 19, 2015 by Clicked

author: Clicked
text:
Straight Versus Tapered Stack MXScandinavia Dyno Testing

 MXScandinavia ran back to back dyno tests on a straight and tapered stack to measure the difference in the shape of the damping force curve. MXScandinavia dyno tested the stacks on a Ohlins four port valve while Jake test rode the stacks on a kx250 shock with a kyb 46 mm valve. From MXScandinavia:

“this is for a Ohlins 46 mx damper and the piston is a 4-port wery similar to the kyb piston.”

 [[IMG:2-valves.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/2-valves.png.94fdf61ae92fc22267f297c2c8f3b142.png]]

 “wery similar”; what the heck does that mean? Click on Google translator and “wery similar: Scandinavian dyno term quantifying valve port geometries as similar, yet different.”

 I make a joke. The thing is, if you are looking for kx250 dyno data this is not it. Wrong valve. The port geometry is similar and the shape of the dyno damping force curve is similar as MXScandinavia says. But the magnitude of the damping force is different, so the dyno data from this test can not be compared to other kx250 data run on an actual kyb valve.

author: Clicked
text:
Dyno Test Results

 By shim factors: the tapered stack has a shim factor of 238 and the straight stack 248. The straight stack should be about 4% stiffer. The MxScandinavia dyno data shows the two stacks tested out to give about the same damping force.  

 [[IMG:3-jake-dyno.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/3-jake-dyno.png.6d95c41e24bb3db03e64d35fe44d6e0c.png]]

 The biggest difference between the two stacks is right around 10 in/sec. At that point the tapered stack is slightly stiffer then the straight stack. That result is odd. Both stacks have the same number of face shims and the same 34.1/28.1 split crossover pair backing the face shims. With everything the same you'd think the stacks would have the same low speed damping, they don't. What the heck is going on there?

author: Clicked
text:
Tapered stack stiffer at low speed

 The straight stack 34.1 mm transition shim has nothing backing it so the stack is clamped on the 28 mm shim. Pretty straight forward.

 On the tapered stack, the 34.1 mm transition shim gets trapped in the crossover gap as the gap closes. So the face shims start out with a 28 mm clamp, just like the straight stack, and transition to a 34 mm clamp as the crossover gap closes. The “trapped” 34.1 crossover makes the tapered stack get stiffer as the crossover closes. In this case the stack is about 8% stiffer at 10 in/sec.  

 [[IMG:4-trapped-co.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/4-trapped-co.png.a0c2d17464f2ea0bef35614a26c3df80.png]]

 As the dyno goes out to higher speeds beyond 10 in/sec the tapered stack gets softer and lines up again with the straight stack around 25 in/sec. What the heck is going on there?

author: mog
text: That just sounds backwards to me ?

author: Clicked
text:
That just sounds backwards to me ?

  

 Yes, it's completely backwards.

 Normally a crossover would be softer at low speed and stiffer at high speed after the crossover gap closes. MXScandinavia demonstrates in the above test a crossover can actually be tuned to be stiffer at low speed through clever use of a “trapped” crossover configuration.

 The stack is only 8% stiffer so no big deal. On the other hand, if you where expecting the crossover to be ~8% softer and it tests out to be 8% stiffer then there is a 16% mystery there. MXScandinavia is showing the “why” of that which I thought was some interesting data.

  

 The more important point here is there is no inherent difference between the shape of the damping force curve for a straight or tapered stack. Both stacks produce a digressive damping force curve with nearly identical damping force values.

 [[IMG:3-jake-dyno.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/3-jake-dyno.png.6d95c41e24bb3db03e64d35fe44d6e0c.png]]

author: Clicked
text:
High Speed Stack Stiffness

 Visually, you might expect the big chunk of shims in the tapered stack high speed section (the 38.25 through 28.25 shims) to be stiffer than the corresponding shims in the straight stack (6x28.25). They are not.  

 [[IMG:5-tapered-section.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/5-tapered-section.png.f831935e7fd5f4cb77aa06f6d2c9c65c.png]]

 By shim factors the tapered stack high speed section (38.25 through 28.25) sum up to a shim factor of 94. The corresponding shims in the straight stack (6x28.25) sum up to a shim factor of 104. That makes the tapered section of the high speed stack 11% softer. So the tapered stack gets progressively softer as the stack is further deflected into the high speed range. That causes the tapered stack damping force to drop down and line up with the straight stack at high speed.

author: Clicked
text:
So if we put a stack of 22s under the cross it should be even stiffer ?instead of the 28s

  

  

 True, but the face shims would then pivot on the 22's instead of the 28's making the face shims softer. So, there is a race going on there between a stiffer high speed stack and softer face shims. Shim factors are clueless on that concept of multiple pivot points.

 For the test here MXScandinavia was after comparison of damping force curve shape. To get the stacks in the same ball park of damping force you have to use 28's for the clamp. 22's would be too soft.

author: Clicked
text:
MXScandinavia Straight v. Tapered Dyno Test

 The MXScandinavia straight versus tapered stack dyno test shows there is no dramatic difference in the shape of the damping force curve between the two stacks. In detail, the tapered stack is stiffer at low speed due to the trapped crossover and softer at high speed due to the softer high speed stack. Those differences are somewhere in the 8% range producing a small effect relative to the straight stack. Overall the damping force curve shape for the two stacks is nearly the same.

 As mog mentioned, a crossover stack is normally softer at low speed and then gets stiffer at high speed after the crossover gap closes. MXScandinavia demonstrates that is not always the case in this dyno test. The crossover stack here is actually stiffer at low speed due to the trapped crossover and softer at high speed due to the softer high speed stack. So there is no universal rule. More importantly, the dyno data demonstrate there is no inherent difference in the shape of the damping force curve between a straight or tapered stack. The MXScandinavia dyno data and FEA analysis both show that.

 [[IMG:3-jake-dyno.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/3-jake-dyno.png.6d95c41e24bb3db03e64d35fe44d6e0c.png]]

author: Clicked
text:
Valving Logic rmz250-152c v. rmz250-248c:

 Valving Logic ran a series of dyno tests looking at the differences in damping force curve shape between a straight and tapered stack. The tests were run on a kyb 46 mm valve for an rmz250 shock. The straight stack has a crossover positioned high in the stack to soften contact with the backer. With that crossover high in the stack the gap makes little difference in the overall stiffness of the stack.  

 [[IMG:6-VL-straight-v-taper-stack.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/6-VL-straight-v-taper-stack.png.9f67b40b2d214ef4ba3b01f9da93a2e8.png]]

 By shim factors the straight stack should be 34% softer then the tapered stack. That is a big difference, what does the dyno say?

author: Clicked
text:
Valving Logic Straight v. Tapered Stack Dyno Data

 The dyno data and FEA analysis both show the two stacks produce nearly identical damping force curves. That is very different than the 34% softer stack expected by shim factors. The data from this Valving Logic test is one of those examples where shim factors fail to estimate the stiffness differences between shim stacks giving results that don't match up with the reality of a test ride.

 [[IMG:7-VL-straight-v-taper-dyno.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/7-VL-straight-v-taper-dyno.png.8b80d0a0c5703b819c1838e4a3fb85fb.png]]

 The more important result and the reason we are looking at this test is the dyno data shows the damping force curve shape for a straight or tapered stack is nearly identical. Both stacks produce a digressive damping force curve with no visible difference in low or high speed damping. The Valving Logic data and MXScandinavia tests both show there is no dramatic damping force curve shape difference between a straight or tapered stack.

author: Clicked
text:
Kawamaha Straight v. Tapered Stacks

 Kawamaha tested straight and tapered stacks using his hydraulic dyno on a yz250 kyb fork valve. Vietze posted those dyno results in a TT thread here. Kawamaha mentions in a different thread the thickness of kyb shims is actually 0.114 mm although he lists them as 0.10 mm. The stacks below list the shims as 0.10 mm because Kawamaha reports them that way, the FEA calculations use the actual shim thickness of 0.114 mm.

 [[IMG:8-kyb24-rebound.png|http://www.shimrestackor.com/TT/4svt/8-kyb24-rebound.png]]

 [[IMG:9-kawa-straight-v-taper-stack.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/9-kawa-straight-v-taper-stack.png.be7fd38bbf2b11e6ad82d157778d6d1a.png]]

 Applying shim factors to the two stacks shows the tapered stack should be 59% stiffer than the straight stack.  

  

 Kawamaha Dyno Data

 By shim factors the tapered stack should be stiffer. The FEA analysis shows the same thing with the tapered stack 12% stiffer. The Kawamaha dyno data shows the opposite result with the tapered stack 12% softer. Results of the test are a riddle.   

 [[IMG:10-kawa-straight-v-taper-dyno.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/10-kawa-straight-v-taper-dyno.png.9f19ade45ea6a06bfb4cf84946913cd3.png]]

 There is no way to figure out the why of that riddle with out more data testing the differences between these stacks. There is no other data on TT testing similar stack configurations so at the point the data simply is what it is.

author: Clicked
text:
Straight Versus Tapered Stack

 From the dyno data on TT:  

MXScandinavia:
 Shim Factors: Straight stack 4% stiffer

 Dyno tests: No difference in damping

 Valving Logic:

 Shim Factors: Straight stack 34% softer

 Dyno tests: No difference in damping

 Kawamaha:

 Shim Factors: Straight stack 59% softer

 Dyno test: Shows opposite result

 The Valving Logic data; MXScandinavia data and FEA analysis all show the same thing. There is no inherent difference in the shape of the damping force curve between a straight or tapered stack. A shim stack could be straight, tapered or an upside down Christmas tree. All that matters is the stiffness the stack structure produces at the face shim. If that stiffness is the same the damping force is going to be the same regardless of the configuration of the shim stack. The dyno data from these tests demonstrate that.

author: Clicked
text:
Why do factories use a tapered stack?

 Manufacturing wise, tapered stacks are a PIA. It is a whole lot easier to buy, stock and assemble straight shim stacks using a single shim diameter. Why do manufactures use tapered stacks?

 Some webology theories:

 The stack has to have a Christmas tree shape to keep the stack from hitting the backer

 You have to taper the stack to soften high speed damping

 The stack has to have a series of large diameter face shims to stiffen low speed damping

 The stack needs to have a range of shim diameters so it can be fine tuned

 Here is another theory: Robustness and Reliability

 On a straight stack all of the shims are forced to bend at the clamp, there is no other pivot. At high deflection the single pivot point at the clamp forces a sharp bend creating a stress concentration point. The sharp bend can push shims beyond the yield point. So, the first time you pile your bike into a whoop face the large blow permanently bends all of the shims at the clamp. Then you have to replace the entire stack. That is time consuming, expensive, and a PIA that gives manufactures a bad rep.

 [[IMG:13-clamp-stress.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/13-clamp-stress.png.367d256765d91992989df275a7ae07b3.png]]

 A tapered stack spreads out the clamp force. The face shims on a tapered stack bend around a larger radius with a smooth arc like shape. At high deflection there is no kink at the clamp creating a stress concentration point. That allows a tapered stack to deflect to higher edge lifts without stressing the shims beyond the yield point. Spreading out the clamp force makes tapered stacks more robust against unexpected large hits. Simple and robust.

 MXScandinavia pointed out that the stacks in older KTM forks had a problem with over stressing shims at the clamp causing the shims to become permanently bent. Re-tuning the stack with a larger taper fixes that.

  

 Just a guess - I think the OEM's use taper for high frequency fatigue life of the shim.
 

 Whether it's high cycle fatigue; low cycle fatigue; tempering or material defects: A tapered stack spreads out the clamp force and reduces stress on the shim. That makes the stack and the shock more robust against unexpected large hits and is the basic reason why shim stacks are tapered.

text:
Absolutely!

  

 TT has a bunch of dyno data for different crossover gap styles. Those stacks are shown back up at the top of this thread. A/B'ing the dyno data from those tests comparing the different crossover gap styles and how changes to the crossover gap configuration effect the shape of the damping force curve leads to some interesting info.

  

  

 Doesn't the tapered stack fit the stacked bowl and fulcrum length theory? It reduces the outside diameter so they remain inside each other as they are forced by fluid pressure to bend as well as the bending point on each shim is at a new reduced diameter as the force placed upon the stack increases.

  

 Kind of lost faith in the stack bowl and fulcrum theories. Those theories made sense against the first couple of dyno tests. But, when we started looking at modifications to the high speed stack the idea that tall stacks are stiffer (the basic premise of the stack bowl and fulcrum theories) kind of fell apart. 

 There does not seem to be a universal rule and there does not seem to be any fundamental difference in the shape of the damping force curve between a straight or tapered stack. That's my read anyway. Looking for some better theories.....

author: Clicked
text:
Back on page 8 we set out with a simple goal comparing straight and tapered stacks trying to answer the question:

  

 Is a straight stack stiffer than a tapered stack?

 First off, what does that question even mean? Like if a stack is stiffer, then it's stiffer. Duh!

 In that sense, this is one of those stupid rhetorical questions that does not have an answer. The question gets asked not to get an answer, but to see if you understand anything about shim stack tuning, or not.

  

 Recast the question in terms of “ride feel” and the dyno data shows tapered and straight stacks both produce digressive damping force curves with nearly identical shapes. The dyno data shows a shim stack could be straight, tapered or an upside down Christmas tree. All that matters is the stiffness of the stack at the face shim. Given that, nearly any shim stack configuration can be manipulated to vary that stiffness over a wide range and produce nearly identical damping force curve shapes. There is no universal rule for one shim stack configuration being stiffer or softer than another.

  

 More importantly, the straight v. tapered dyno tests are consistent with the previous dyno tests showing changes to the low speed or high speed stack do not change the shape of the damping force curve. Those stack modifications simply make the stack stiffer or softer. Changing the damping force curve shape requires manipulation of other features in the shim stack. The dyno data here on TT shows you how to do that and we will get to that data. The first step is looking at the various webology approaches to shim stack tuning to see if they work out or not when compared to dyno data.

			
				

	Edited September 22, 2015 by Clicked

author: Clicked
text:
Shim Stack Tuning Webology:

 So far, this thread has looked at six points of shim stack tuning webology. Some theories have worked out, others have not. Here is a summary of webology theories verified with dyno data so far:  

 Shims become stiffer at edge lifts greater than one shim thickness

 False: The MXScandinavia finger press data shows shim stiffness is nearly linear out to edge lifts of 7 shim thicknesses. For a shock that is equivalent to a wheel speed of 38 m/sec and well beyond the 7 to 10 m/sec speeds generally considered to be the extremes of MX suspension velocities. If you can not see any effect at 38 m/sec it just is not going to show up in a suspension system

 Shim stiffness becomes nonlinear at high lift

 False: The MXScandinavia finger press data shows shim stiffness is nearly linear out to edge lifts of 7 shim thicknesses. Data from that test is equivalent to hitting a 7 inch bump at 140 mph 

 A second point here: the data shows shim stiffness is “nearly” linear. It is not “exactly” linear, but far close to linear than the strong non-linear effects commonly expected based on Belleville springs

 A tall stack of thin shims is stiffer than a short stack of thick shims

 False: The stacked bowl theory and fulcrum theory both assert tall stacks are stiffer. Those theories made sense against the first two MXScandinavia dyno tests modifying the low and high speed stack. Further tests changing the height of the high speed stack did not support the theory. So “sometimes” tall stacks are stiffer, sometimes they are not. Rules that only work sometimes just aren't very useful for suspension tuning

 A tall stack of thin shims is more progressive than a short stack of thick shims

 True: The stacked bowl theory asserts shims added to the top of the stack are force to bend around a sharper bend radius. That theory supports the dyno data showing tall stacks of thin shims are stiffer, demonstrated by the SF4/SF14 finger press data comparison

Stiffer high speed stacks increase high speed damping
False: Increasing the stiffness of the high speed stack makes the damping stiffer everywhere, not just at high speed. The Ohlins dyno data, the MXScandinavia dyno data and the FEA analysis all show that effect

 A straight stack is stiffer than a tapered stack

 False: Shim stacks can be straight, tapered or an upside down Christmas tree. All that matters is the stiffness the stack structure produces at the face shim. The Valving Logic data and MXScandinavia data both demonstrate there is no difference in the shape of the damping force curve between a straight or tapered stack

 There may be other dyno data out there showing some of these webology theories work. The dyno data here shows they do not work. Theories that only work sometimes just aren't very useful for suspension tuning.

author: Clicked
text:
Crossover Tuning:

 How much does a crossover change the damping force curve? Valving Logic set out to answer that question by adding a crossover to a simple tapered shim stack. The baseline stack, rmz250-248c, uses a simple tapered shim stack on a kyb 46 mm shock valve. The second test, rmz250-249c, adds a single 24.15 crossover behind the face shims to see how much the damping force curve changes.

 [[IMG:1-crossover.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/1-crossover.png.fdcddc66844b4196a97fc8b82528bc73.png]]

 The crossover gap allows the face shims to crack open and deflect independently from the rest of the stack. The port edge lift curve computed above demonstrates the effect. From zero to 30 lbf on the stack the crossover stack (green curve) deflects more. Higher edge deflection softens low speed damping for the crossover stack.

  

 After the crossover gap closes the face shims are in contact with the high speed stack. Further deflection of the stack now requires the entire stack to deflect. That makes the stack stiffer and gives the crossover stack the same stiffness as the baseline stack at high speed. The parallel lines for the two stacks at high speed, above 30 lbf, means the stiffness is the same. Same slope, means they have the same stiffness.

  

 While the stiffness is the same at high speed, the flow area of the crossover stack is larger because the face shims are deflected across the crossover gap. That gives the crossover stack more flow area and softer damping. So while the stiffness of the two shim stacks are the same at high speed, the larger flow area of the crossover stack makes the crossover stack softer.

  

 The dyno results from this test show adding a crossover gap makes low speed damping softer. That is a very important tuning tool. Exploiting that capability has created many different crossover styles with subtle differences in the crossover geometry effecting shim stack stiffness and the way the stack transitions from low speed to high speed damping.

  

 TT has a bunch of dyno data demonstrating performance of different crossover styles.

author: Clicked
text:
Valve Geometries:

 About half of the valves used in the dyno test on TT are “free flowing” (rebound ports) and the other half are “non-free flowing”. The “non-free flowing” geometries are the compression side of the valve. So there is a bunch of data here for both "free flowing" and "non-free flowing" types valves.

 [[IMG:b1-TT-dyno-valves.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/b1-TT-dyno-valves.png.fcb0bf2795786398656ce1c49b1b5f05.png]]

  

 Valve Port Geometry:

 [[IMG:b2-kyb46mm-rebound.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/b2-kyb46mm-rebound.png.b0b5280bc524076e28399672f5fa1276.png]]

 The parameters r.port, d.port and w.port define the spill  paths out of the valve. Those parameters also define the valve pocket area, the pressurized surface on the shim stack face and the forces deflecting the shim stack.

  

 On the compression side the same parameters (r.port, d.port and w.port) define the dimensions of the pressurized valve pocket area. Compression valves usually also have a  valve port flow restriction defined by d.thrt. The port restriction produces a fluid jet acting on the outer perimeter of the shim stack to create the effects bbatarelo was talking about above.

 [[IMG:b3-kyb46mm-compression.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/b3-kyb46mm-compression.png.9547045134d2c98771190710e2ba32a7.png]]

 On a large hit all of the flow through the valve is forced to flow through the d.thrt flow restriction. That causes the valve port to hydraulically lock up at high speed. imo, the primary reason manufactures put flow restrictions on compression pistons is to keep the shock from blowing through it’s stroke on a large hit.

  

 Entrance Flow Restriction:

 Another flow restriction you will see on suspension valves is a restriction at the port entrance. The entrance flow area is defined by h.deck measured between the valve deck and first shim on the reverse flow shim stack. That deck height area is often smaller than the valve throat and limits the flow at high speed.

  

 KTM fork valves are built with a low deck height for that reason. Delta shims are used on those valves  to space the shim stack off of the valve face and open up the flow area. Imo, that is a better approach then  a valve port flow restriction because the deck height is easily tunable by changing the delta shims. To retune a valve port flow restriction you have to fill up the valve port with JB weld and then re-drill a smaller throat.

 [[IMG:b4-hdeck.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/b4-hdeck.png.3298e1d447e2b474a7fb3a2fd924997f.png]]

  

  

  

 [[IMG:b5-bbatarelo-valves.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/b5-bbatarelo-valves.png.b5fa7299b4b8f3be10725d2fb29b584b.png]]

  

 For the valves bbatarelo shows the definitions of the r.port, d.port and w.port look pretty straight forward to me. For d.thrt, the port web on the Race Tech valve looks like something done for manufacturing convenience more then control of port flow area. There does not seem to be enough port web thickness in there to worry about. To get the calculations to ignore d.thrt set it to zero.

  

 Coming at this the other way, the Race Tech valve looks to have 100 times the port flow area of that Showa valve. So the Race Tech valve is not going to hit any flow limitations until suspension velocities pretty far beyond what Showa was thinking about for that shock application.

  

 Those valves all look pretty much the same with the exception of the showa HMAS valve. That valve is running a large seat width around the port.

 [[IMG:b6-showa-valve.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/b6-showa-valve.png.c9eca58381fd85d67f14c6c8d86e4c3a.png]]

 At low speed when the shim stack is barely cracked open, the flow is forced through a very small slit between the valve seat and shim stack. When the valve has a wide seat, like the one above, that creates a large surface area and high viscous losses. Those viscous losses increase low speed damping. As the shim stack lifts further the flow area increases and the viscous losses go away.

  

 Fox used this same approach on their new RE:aktiv mountain bike shock. A large seat width and increased low speed damping was used to keep the bike from bobbing on pedal strokes.

author: Clicked
text:
One Thing At A Time

 The usual thinking for tuning is only change one thing at a time. Test ride the bike, see what it “feels” like and make corrections before things get too far out of hand. That makes sense.

 [[IMG:1a-one-thing.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/1a-one-thing.png.8fdd53889b0f18ccd4dfe6e50a9e866f.png]]

 That is a problem for crossover tuning. Put a crossover in the stack and the damping force changes everywhere, both a low speed and at high speed. Test ride the above setup and the dyno shows the damping force is flat too soft everywhere.

  

 To get to “one thing at a time” changes in the damping force curve you have to add a bunch of shims to the stack tapered section to get the high speed damping back into the range of the original stack. For the stack tested above that requires doubling every shim in the stack taper.  

 [[IMG:1b-one-thing-damping.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/1b-one-thing-damping.png.a0ef7e7ac56706aeea0d798ca646c068.png]]

 So here is the dilemma for crossover tuning:  

 Change one thing at a time in the shim stack and everything in the damping force curve changes. Test ride that and the entire damping force curve is mucked up

 To get to “one thing at a time” changes in the damping force curve you have to make a bunch of changes to the shim stack so that only one part of the damping force curve gets changed at a time

 Dyno's were invented for that very reason. With a dyno you can add or remove a crossover and then hack around on the rest of the shim stack so that only one part of the damping force curve gets changed. Test ride that and you can “feel” if the change in the damping force curve went in the right direction and fine tune it. That keeps you from wasting a bunch of time test riding wacky shim stacks that are way off the mark.

  

 Tuning “one thing at a time” makes sense. The problem is getting to a “one thing at a time” change in the damping force curve ends up requiring a bunch of simultaneous changes to the shim stack – and that gets tricky.

text:
Non-Interactive Crossovers:

 Jeremy Wilkey on Dirt Rider defines Independent and Non-independent as the two basic styles of crossovers. I refer to those as Non-Interactive and Interactive. Same thing, different lingo.

  

 Non-interactive crossovers are the configurations tuners talk about when describing how a crossover effects the damping force of a shock. Non-interactive crossovers use a shim diameter that is smaller than the stack clamp. That allows the face shims to deflect independently from the rest of the stack up to the point where the crossover gap closes. After that the entire stack deflects making the stack stiffer at high speed. The operation of a non-interactive crossover is pretty straight forward.

  

 John Curea's dyno test of the Dogger's crf450r rebound stack demonstrates operation of a non-interactive crossover. The dyno test was run on a Showa 50 oval shock valve.

 [[IMG:3-showa50ovalR.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/3-showa50ovalR.png.e3c54c21ca76d8f5e8fb83cda366e829.png]]

author: Clicked
text:
Interactive Crossovers:

 Jeremy Wilkey defines the second type of crossover as an interactive crossover. Interactive crossovers use a shim diameter that is larger than the stack clamp. When the crossover is larger than the clamp some of the force on the face shims is transferred directly through the crossover shim into the high speed stack. The transferred force causes the high speed stack to start deflecting before the crossover gap closes. Mog's stack dyno tested by MXScandinavia on a four port Ohlins valve is an example of an interactive crossover.

 [[IMG:4-interactive-co.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/4-interactive-co.png.088d752453c19580dc90a9a21294a781.png]]

 To close the crossover gap the face shims have to “chase down” the moving/deflecting high speed stack on an interactive crossover. That delays closure of the crossover gap and spreads out the crossover closure “event” over a range of shaft velocities. Mog's stack shows those effects. There is no kink in the stack deflection curve when the crossover gap closes and no kink in the damping force curve measured on the dyno for that stack.

 [[IMG:5-mog01.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/5-mog01.png.c49b9dc00c899feb13b06a83fe138d86.png]]

 Interactive crossovers have no distinct “event” when the crossover gap closes. Instead, the process is spread out over a range of shaft velocities. That introduces the idea of “mid-speed” damping where the damping force is somewhere in between the low speed force, defined by the face shims, and high speed force defined by the stiffness of the entire stack.

  

 Why do we see so few of these (non-interactive crossovers) types of stacks ?they seem better focused at the individual stages of ls and hs , I've only seem one oem with this a 04 rm

  

 Why so few non-interactive crossovers?

 Non-interactive crossovers have a well defined low speed and high speed stack separated by the crossover gap. That makes a lot of tuning sense, but creates a sharp transition when the crossover closes. Jeremy Wilkey points out that creates a shock that works “well” on one series of bumps but on the next series of slightly larger bumps the crossover closes and the shock suddenly gets too stiff.  

  

 The fix is an interactive crossover to spread out the transition and produce a more consistent feel across the shaft velocity range. That's the theory – in practice tuning gets tricky.

author: Clicked
text:
This stack did ride like it had a very smooth transition ,it was very plush with a consistent response to bumps ,however I was comparing to a 05 rmz wuth it's ancient shock and funny linkage ,it might not be so great compared to a more modern bike

 Cool to see theory work out in practice once in awhile...

  

 Above, Jeremy Wilkey defined two basic types of crossovers: Interactive and non-interactive. Beyond those basic configurations the dyno data on TT demonstrates use of two additional types of crossovers: Trapped crossovers and “fo” crossovers.

  

 Trapped Crossovers:

 Instead of a single shim, trapped crossovers use a pair of shims with different diameters to form the crossover gap. As the crossover closes the larger shim gets “trapped” in the crossover gap. That causes the face shims to start out with a small clamp diameter and shift to a larger clamp when the second shim gets trapped in the closing crossover gap. The change in clamp diameter causes the low speed damping start out soft and transition to a stiffer rate as the crossover closes.

 MXScandinavia dyno testing of the Jake Normal stack demonstrates use of a trapped crossover.

 [[IMG:6-jake-normal.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/6-jake-normal.png.cfbd4d5be5ddbfad02fb9224a9ed3218.png]]

author: Clicked
text:
"fo" Crossovers:

 The fourth type of crossover is a “fo” crossover. “fo” crossovers, like “fo” fur, are fake and create a crossover gap that never closes. “fo” crossovers are generated by crossover shim diameters that are too large or high speed stacks that are too soft. When the crossover diameter is too large too much force is transferred through the crossover into the high speed stack. That forces the high speed stack to deflect at the same rate as the face shims so the “fo” gap never closes. “fo” crossovers do nothing other than cause confusion. MXScandinavia shows some examples.

 [[IMG:7-fo-mx2c.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/7-fo-mx2c.png.f7121c003ae6f4f90b662f4c766c5365.png]]

 “fo” gaps are sensitive to changes in the shim stack configuration. For example on the above stack: If you reduce the crossover shim diameter a tad, less force is transferred through the crossover into the high speed stack. That reduces the high speed stack deflection and converts what was a “fo” crossover into a regular interactive crossover.

 [[IMG:8-fo-fix.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/8-fo-fix.png.f31ae01ec318208bcb975dea8adfaac6.png]]

 Crossovers that flip into and out of a “fo” configuration drive dyno tuners crazy. With only minor changes to the stack taper or clamp a crossover can flop over into a “fo” configuration causing the whole damping force curve to flop over into a different shape – often by a bunch.

 Those sudden shifts in the stack behavior lead to all kinds of wacky dyno based conclusions like non-linear shim forces or complex three dimensional fluid dynamics dominating the shocks performance. Worse, it prevents you from getting the damping profile you wanted, not because the shim stack was bad, but because things were going on in the stack nobody understood when dyno testing the shock. “fo” crossovers flipping into and out of an active configuration can wasting weeks of dyno test time trying to figure out what is going on in the stack.

author: Clicked
text:
Crossover Styles:

 The dyno data on TT demonstrates use of four different crossover styles:

 [[IMG:8a-styles.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/8a-styles.png.8cf2ff660b4a731970c6835cf25b3d73.png]]

 There is a bunch of dyno data on TT demonstrating use of each type of crossover. The next step is digging through the data to find examples. Take a look at how each style effects low speed and high speed damping. And then try to figure out when you would want to use one crossover style over another.

author: Clicked
text:
Non-Interactive Crossover Configurations

 The dyno data on TT shows some of examples of non-interactive crossovers. We'll take a look at a few here and more latter comparing the effects of different crossover styles.  

  

 crf450r Dogger rebound

 John Curea, using the Mx Tech dyno, ran a couple of dyno tests helping the Dogger setup his crf450r rebound stack on the Showa 50 oval port valve used in that shock. The Dogger's rebound stack had a conventional non-interactive crossover with a shim diameter smaller than the stack clamp. The configuration allows the face shims to deflect independently from the high speed stack. The stack deflection curve shows the behavior you would expect for a non-interactive crossover: Soft at low speed until the crossover closes and a sudden transition to a stiffer rate after that point.  

 [[IMG:9-dogger-rbnd.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/9-dogger-rbnd.png.9d4384317cb6b5af121a7d495f28c2ab.png]]

 Normally, the stack face shims hold the valve port closed at low speed. When the valve port is closed all of the flow is forced through the clicker bleed circuits driving low speed damping forces up. But, the Dogger's stack only had four face shims. The soft face shims allowed the valve port to blow open at low speed so the flow bypassed the clicker bleed circuits. The end result is the stack produced little low speed damping making a damping force curve that was nearly linear all the way down to a shaft speed of zero.

author: Clicked
text:
So is this desirable ?a linear force curve ?

  

 No, a linear damping curve is not desirable. Agree with tmsuspension.

  

 Here's the theory:

 250 lb bike, 180 lb rider, 40/60 weight split. Take off 50 lbs for the front wheel and another 50 for the rear and the rear chassis weight is around 200 lbs. At 200 lbs the chassis needs some stiff damping for motion control, but at the same time the 50 lb wheels need to float over bumps.

  

 The shock's performance has to simultaneously satisfy two conflicting requirements: Stiff damping to control the chassis and soft damping to float the wheel over bumps. The shock can't do both, it is one or the other.

  

 The usual compromise is tune the shock to produce stiff damping at low speed for chassis control, and soft damping at high speed to control the wheels. That creates a damping profile with a “knee” in the curve marking the point where the shock transitions from low speed chassis damping to high speed wheel damping. Wipe out the knee and the chassis becomes a wallowing mess. Wrap your head around that and you will go far in suspension tuning.

  

 That's the basic theory. But on the other hand, the wheel has to punch through all of that low speed damping every time you hit a bump. Too much low speed and the ride gets harsh – not enough and the chassis wallows. Suspension tuning is all about controlling that transition and positioning the “knee” to generate enough low speed damping to control the chassis and transitioning out of that range fast enough so the ride doesn't get harsh.

  

 On the rebound side harsh means packing. Most rebound stacks use a crossover to back off on the low speed a bit and prevent packing. Go to stiffer springs and the low speed damping can be increased a bit without packing up the rebound stroke -or stated the other way – stiffer springs require stiffer rebound to keep control of the chassis and the wheels as well.

author: Clicked
text:
John Curea Stack Mod For Stiffer Spring Rate

 Based on the shim stack configuration and dyno test Curea suspected the rebound was too soft and recommended two mods: Increase low speed damping to handle the Dogger's 270 lb weight; and increase high speed damping to handle the Dogger's stiffer spring rates.

  

 To get more low speed damping Curea added five more face shims. The stiffer face shims kept the valve ports closed longer forcing the flow to be “on the clickers” at low speed to increase low speed damping. At high speed Curea wanted 10% more rebound damping to handle the stiffer springs. To get a 10% high speed increase Curea had to actually soften the high speed stack to compensate for the stiffer face shims. Curea's dyno test shows the combination of softer high speed and stiffer low speed results in an overall high speed damping force increase of 10%.

 [[IMG:10-curea-rbnd.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/10-curea-rbnd.png.40e16740adf50d8ac17870174b80aea3.png]]

 The stiffer stack face shims John Curea used moved the crossover closure point out to 5 in/sec compared to 3 in/sec for the Dogger's original setup. That increased the low speed damping by about 40% at 5 in/sec. At high speed the softer clamp used in Curea's stack softened the high speed damping so the overall increase at high speed was only about 10%. 

  

 Earlier, MXScandinavia tested interactive crossover stacks and showed increasing the low speed stack stiffness increased the damping force everywhere, both at low speed and at high speed. Likewise, increasing the high speed stack stiffness increased damping force everywhere across the speed range. In this test Curea shows that if you stiffen the low speed stack AND soften the high speed stack you can actually change the low speed damping force curve relative to the high speed. But you've got to simultaneously change both parts of the stack to make that work. That gets confusing if you've got a “one thing at a time” approach to shim stack tuning.

  

 The other thing John Curea shows in this test is the behavior of the crossover gap changed when the stack got re-tuned. The shaft velocity where the crossover gap closed got shifted and the abruptness or “kink” in the stack deflection curve got smoothed out. Same crossover, same crossover gap, but the two stacks are going to “feel” different on a test ride with the crossover gap transition smoothed out.

author: Clicked
text:
John Curea yz250

 Curea posted a second non-interactive crossover example for a stock yz250 shock. In this case the crossover shim diameter is slightly larger than the stack clamp. That makes the configuration an interactive crossover by Jeremy Wilkey's definition. But in this case, the low speed stack is soft and the high speed stack is stiff. So the forces transferred through the crossover shim are not enough to start deflection the high speed stack before the crossover closes. You can see that in the stack deflection plot. Since the high speed stack does not deflect until the crossover closes the configuration basically behaves like a non-interactive crossover.  

 [[IMG:11-curea-yz250R.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/11-curea-yz250R.png.610c8eb99798fdfe176b29e9df459d42.png]]

 You'd like to have hard and fast rules for shim stack tuning like the definitions of interactive and non-interactive crossover gaps. But, shim stack behavior often ends up being an “it depends” kind of deal. For the above stack, the stiffness of the low speed stack relative to the high speed stack turned out to be more important then the small diameter difference between the crossover and stack clamp. So the stack ends up behaving like a regular non-interactive crossover instead of an interactive crossover. The dyno test above is one of those examples where one parameter ends up dominating over another and the stack behavior ends up being different than the hard and fast rules you might of had in mind when assembling the stack.

author: Clicked
text:
Valving Logic rmz250 Shock Compression:

 Valving Logic has also posted examples of non-interactive crossovers on TT. This rmz250 shock compression stack was run on a kyb 46mm valve. The stack has a crossover diameter slightly larger than the stack clamp, so by the numbers the stack was an interactive crossover configuration. But the stack deflection plot does not show any deflection of the high speed stack at the point where the crossover closes. So the stack actually behaves like a non-interactive crossover.

  

 Either way, the change in stack stiffness at the point where the crossover closes was small and did not produce any real change in damping force measured for the shock. In that respect the test data shows it did not really matter whether the crossover was an interactive or non-interactive configuration.

 [[IMG:12-rmz250-249c.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/12-rmz250-249c.png.cc256ff2556defee99ec1952cb065dea.png]]

author: Clicked
text:
Valving Logic rm85 Shock Compression Stack

 Here is a second example from Valving Logic for a rm85 shock. This stack also uses a crossover diameter larger than the stack clamp making the stack a potential interactive crossover configuration. But, the face shims in the stack are soft and deflect across the crossover gap before enough force is transferred through the crossover shim to begin deflection of the high speed stack.

  

 The stack here uses a crossover shim that is 30% larger than the stack clamp. But still behaves like a non-interactive crossover because the high speed stack is stiff.

 [[IMG:13-showa40c-valve.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/13-showa40c-valve.png.7285059258f5e9ed4e02507522e9fdd5.png]]

 At the point where the crossover closes the stack graphic shows no deflection of the high speed stack. An interactive crossover configuration would be slightly deflected.

author: Clicked
text:
The idea of the crossover shim diameter defining the difference between active and non-interactive crossover gaps is straight forward. Implementing that in practice gets tricky because the crossover gap behavior depends on the crossover shim diameter and the stiffness of the low speed stack relative to the high speed stack. The last three dyno tests show examples where an interactive crossover gap configuration ended up testing out as non-interactive gap because the low speed stack was much softer than the high speed stack. So you have to consider both the crossover gap configuration and stack stiffness to figure out how a crossover gap is going to behave.

  

 Stack Float

 One more non-interactive crossover gap configuration from Kawamaha. This stack is for a yz250 fork compression valve. The stack uses a very thick crossover shim with a diameter that is larger than the stack clamp. That makes the stack a potential interactive crossover configuration. But, the crossover shim is very thick and stiff so it does not bend at all. That makes the configuration behave like a regular non-interactive crossover.

  

 Looking at the shim stack configuration plot it is obvious the crossover shim in that stack is not going to bend. That is not so obvious if you are just looking at a listing of shims used in the stack.

 [[IMG:15-kawa-stack.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/15-kawa-stack.png.8791010d2a8aff5679a5efce730166ac.png]]

 The above shim stack also has float. Because of the float and the crossover gap there are two events in the dyno curve. One when the stack float opens against the check spring and a second when the crossover gap closes. Those events put two inflection points in the dyno curve.

 [[IMG:16-kawa-dyno-comp.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/16-kawa-dyno-comp.png.aabad34250f1e6af49eba31a08346b0a.png]]

author: Clicked
text:
[[IMG:8a-styles.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/8a-styles.png.8cf2ff660b4a731970c6835cf25b3d73.png]]

 Interactive Crossover Configurations

 MXScandinavia shows some examples of interactive crossover configurations. Interactive crossovers use a crossover shim diameter that is larger than the stack clamp. The larger crossover shim transfers some of the force on the face shims directly into the high speed stack before the crossover closes. That starts deflection of the high speed stack before the crossover closes, spreads out the closing event and shifts the crossover closure point to a higher shaft velocity.  

 [[IMG:17-ohlins-rbnd.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/17-ohlins-rbnd.png.4824e9859dca573662f09e54ab987bc1.png]]

 The final stack in that test series, mx5r, actually has a “fo” gap. That is why it falls out of family with the other stacks.

  

 On an interactive crossover the larger diameter crossover shim adds more support to the face shims making the face shims stiffer. That adds low speed damping. The larger diameter crossover shim also transfers some of the force on the face shims directly into the high speed stack. That forces the high speed stack to begin deflecting before the crossover closes and softens the crossover closure “event”. The end result is a smooth damping force curve with no distinct “kink” or event at the point where the crossover closes.

  

 There more example of interactive crossover gaps in the dyno data on TT, most of the dyno examples are actually configured that way.

author: Clicked
text:
MXScandinavia Jake01 Stack:

 The Jake01 stack tested by MXScandinavia is an example of an interactive crossover. The stack deflection curve shows the crossover closure is spread out over a range of shaft velocities with no distinct event in the damping force measurement when the crossover closes. The stack produces a smooth digressive damping force curve.

 [[IMG:18-jake01.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/18-jake01.png.ab28fd65322b0b000d6a53e4fc8f12a5.png]]

author: Clicked
text:
MXScandinavia Jake01 Stack:

 More detail on the Jake01 dyno curve. To understand why the dyno curve is shaped the way it is you have to look at the shim stack, shim stack flow area and damping force curve to figure out what is going on in the flow circuits to chage the shape of the damping force curve. The shock tested here transitions from low speed damping, dominated by the clicker bleed circuit, to shim stack control at a shaft velocity around 5 in/sec. That is the “knee” in the low speed damping force curve.  

 [[IMG:18b-co-close.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/18b-co-close.png.b18ffb923e94059e7575e7638364f212.png]]

 At 5 in/sec the stack flow area curve shows the flow area through the shim stack is about equal to the flow area through the clicker bleed circuit. So the flow split at the “knee” is something like 50/50 between the stack and bleed circuit. As the shaft velocity advances beyond that point the bleed circuit has progressively less influence since the flow area through the shim stack is larger.

  

 Drag the slide bar on the shim stack up to the point where the crossover closes and the flow area curve shows there is about 60 lbf of fluid force on the stack. That occurs at a shaft velocity around 35 in/sec. But, drawing a straight line through the high speed stack flow area curve shows the stack does not really get into the high speed range until there is about 100 lbf of fluid force on the stack. To get 100 lbf of fluid force the shaft velocity needs to be around 65 in/sec. So the interactive crossover used in this stack has a transition range from 35 to 65 in/sec. Through that range the stack transitions from the mid-speed damping, defined by the stiffness of the face shims, to high speed damping defined by the stiffness of the entire stack.

 [[IMG:18a-co-close.png|//cdn.thumpertalk.com/uploads/imageproxy/18a-co-close.png.2bb0dbe7034445c5a3db9904e6366739.png]]

 Unfortunately MXScandinavia's dyno only had enough power to push the shock to a damping force of 600 lbf at a shaft velocity of 40 in/sec. So we never got to see how the shim stack behaved in the high speed range above 65 in/sec. To get that data the dyno would have to be able to push a shock with 1,000 lbf of damping force out to shaft velocities beyond 65 in/sec.

  

 Lack of dyno power is a common problem testing automotive shocks. It's tough to get enough power to push those shocks beyond 20 in/sec. For those situations all you get is low speed data and you can't see how the shim stack transitions into high speed damping or how the shock performs after all of the crossover gaps in the stack are closed. Data taken in that transition range can lead to all kinds of wacky dyno conclusions because the dyno is not measuring the stiffness of the shim stack, it is measuring the stiffness of the crossover closure transition and that often has little to do with the overall stiffness of the stack.
